titleStmt.title: Have We Forgotten Auditory Sensory Memory? Retention Intervals in Studies of Nonverbal Auditory Working Memory
titleStmt.author: Nees

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Have We Forgotten Auditory Sensory Memory? Retention Intervals in Studies of Nonverbal Auditory Working Memory

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The retention intervals used in nonverbal auditory working-memory experiments, and whether they are long enough to exclude auditory sensory memory.
span.quote: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded

span.label: When a study reports working memory for a nonverbal sound after a few seconds, is it measuring working memory at all, or the sensory trace that persists alongside it?
span.quote: The retention interval must extend beyond the persistence of ASM to isolate WM processes, because information about the most recently heard stimulus is simultaneously available to both ASM and WM (e.g., rehearsal) processes.

span.label: Shows that the conventional 3-5 s retention interval does not exclude auditory sensory memory, so a body of findings attributed to working memory is ambiguous between two constructs.
span.quote: This conflation of different constructs may be one contributor to discrepant research findings and the resulting proliferation of theoretical conjectures regarding mechanisms of working memory for nonverbal sounds.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Unlike verbal working memory studies that use serial recall tasks, research paradigms for exploring nonverbal working memory—especially two-stimulus comparison tasks—may not be differentiating working memory from sensory memory processes in analyses of behavioral responses, because retention interval durations have not excluded the possibility that the sensory memory trace drives task performance.

span.label: nonverbal auditory working memory
span.quote: Researchers have shown increased interest in mechanisms of working memory for nonverbal sounds such as music and environmental sounds.

span.label: review
span.quote: This assumption is examined in detail in this comment.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: during a short retention interval the lingering sensory trace and the rehearsed working-memory trace remain available in parallel, so the participant can answer from either, and the experimenter cannot attribute performance to one store
span.quote: With Retention Interval A, the participant could consult either the lingering ASM trace 1 or the rehearsed WM trace to decide whether the standard and comparison stimuli are the same or different; both memory traces exist in parallel.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: sensory memory keeps task performance intact when rehearsal is blocked, so a genuinely interfering secondary task can still yield a null result that is then misread as showing the two tasks use different mechanisms
span.quote: Even when the WM rehearsal mechanism for a stimulus has been blocked, task performance may remain partially or even fully intact due to contributions from ASM (e.g., McKeown et al., 2011 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the two memories run in parallel, so while the sensory trace survives, either one can drive the response and the experiment cannot tell which did
span.quote: The retention interval must extend beyond the persistence of ASM to isolate WM processes, because information about the most recently heard stimulus is simultaneously available to both ASM and WM (e.g., rehearsal) processes.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the convention arose from an early estimate that the sensory trace lasted about two seconds, which later work did not support
span.quote: Researchers initially speculated that the maximum duration of the ASM trace was about 2 s or less (e.g., Neisser, 1967 ; Crowder, 1976 ), which suggested that negligible contributions of ASM to memory performance could be assumed when intervals exceeded 2 s.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: the verbal literature escaped the problem because serial recall lets primacy and recency separate rehearsal from the sensory trace; nonverbal sounds cannot be recalled aloud, so that separation is unavailable
span.quote: Nonverbal sounds typically are not amenable to recall tasks, because participants would need to respond verbally

span.label: The paper cannot prescribe a retention-interval duration that would definitively remove auditory sensory memory, because estimates of that memory's duration vary too widely.
span.quote: The indeterminate duration of ASM precludes recommending a definitive retention interval duration that would eliminate contributions of ASM.

span.label: The alternative remedy the paper discusses - overwriting the sensory trace with an irrelevant sound - lacks the empirical evidence needed to justify assuming it works.
span.quote: Overwriting in ASM requires more research, but without definitive empirical evidence, it seems unwarranted to assume that a noise burst or a composite stimulus will eliminate contributions of ASM to WM tasks.

span.label: The paper is a commentary: it identifies an interpretive ambiguity and does not measure how much of any published effect is actually sensory.
span.quote: Researchers seem to have assumed that sensory memory has a negligible impact on performance in auditory two-stimulus comparison tasks. This assumption is examined in detail in this comment.

span.label: The critique rests on duration estimates that themselves vary by a factor of thirty, so it cannot say which interval would be long enough.
span.quote: Research has shown striking variation in the estimated duration of ASM.

span.label: auditory sensory memory
span.quote: Thus, ASM is a passive store of just-heard sounds that retains a “synthesized auditory memory” ( Massaro, 1975 )

span.label: echoic memory
span.quote: Neisser (1967) dubbed the auditory sensory store echoic memory —a term synonymous with auditory sensory memory (ASM).

span.label: working memory
span.quote: These “working” aspects of WM— active mental manipulation, rehearsal, and reinstatement of information— represent an important functional distinction between WM and ASM.

span.label: short-term store
span.quote: Auditory sensory memory is qualitatively different from post-sensory memory processes ( Massaro, 1972 ; Crowder, 1982 ), including Atkinson and Shiffrin’s short-term store, which evolved into the working memory (WM) construct (see, e.g., Logie and Cowan, 2015 ).

span.label: sensory register
span.quote: Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) influential memory model described a sensory register , a short-term store , and a long-term store .

span.label: retention interval
span.quote: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded

span.label: two-stimulus comparison tasks
span.quote: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded

span.label: serial recall
span.quote: Thus, in the verbal WM literature, the respective contributions of WM rehearsal and ASM have been disentangled in empirical investigations and their accompanying theoretical interpretations (see Jones et al., 2004 , 2006 ).

span.label: mismatch negativity
span.quote: The widely researched mismatch negativity (MMN) component (see Näätänen, 2000 ) of evoked neural responses to sounds offers a metric of the duration of ASM.

span.label: rehearsal
span.quote: ASM does not involve active manipulation or rehearsal (see, especially, Green and McKeown, 2007 , Experiment 2; also see McKeown and Mercer, 2012 ) and is insensitive to attentional processes

span.label: auditory imagery
span.quote: Further, ASM is only engaged when a sound is heard, whereas WM for sounds can be initiated in the absence of hearing a stimulus (i.e., when a sound is reinstated from long-term memory, as in auditory imagery).

span.label: memory - the passive sensory kind: a high-resolution trace of what was just heard, not manipulable and not under attentional control
span.quote: Thus, ASM is a passive store of just-heard sounds that retains a “synthesized auditory memory” ( Massaro, 1975 )

span.label: memory - the working kind: active manipulation, rehearsal and reinstatement, able to run without any sound having been heard
span.quote: These “working” aspects of WM— active mental manipulation, rehearsal, and reinstatement of information— represent an important functional distinction between WM and ASM.

span.label: short-term memory - used loosely as a synonym for working memory, which the paper identifies as part of how the two constructs got conflated
span.quote: Auditory sensory memory is qualitatively different from post-sensory memory processes ( Massaro, 1972 ; Crowder, 1982 ), including Atkinson and Shiffrin’s short-term store, which evolved into the working memory (WM) construct (see, e.g., Logie and Cowan, 2015 ).

span.label: contradicts → Golubock and Janata (2013)
span.quote: Golubock and Janata (2013) defined retention of a sound for as brief as 1 s following stimulation as a WM task.

span.label: contradicts → Soemer and Saito (2015)
span.quote: Using retention intervals as brief as 3 s, Soemer and Saito (2015) likewise implied that the retention of a sound for any duration following stimulation must be accomplished by an active WM maintenance mechanism (also see Schulze et al., 2012 ). Schendel and Palmer (2007) used a 4.2 s retention interval in their study of mechanisms of WM for melodies. Li et al. (2013) and Siedenburg and McAdams (2016) used 6 s retention intervals in studies of nonverbal auditory WM. Though sounds may indeed engage WM processes immediately following perception, parallel access to ASM also may have influenced task performance in some studies that attempted to examined WM processes. Is this apparent oversight semantic or substantive?

span.label: contradicts → studies treating any post-stimulus retention as working memory, e.g. Golubock and Janata (2013)
span.quote: Golubock and Janata (2013) defined retention of a sound for as brief as 1 s following stimulation as a WM task.

span.label: builds-on → Schröger's (2007) review of mismatch negativity studies
span.quote: In a review of MMN studies, Schröger (2007) concluded that ASM may endure up to 20 s or longer.

span.label: builds-on → Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968) three-store memory model
span.quote: Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) influential memory model described a sensory register , a short-term store , and a long-term store .

span.label: echoic memory —same-as→ auditory sensory memory
span.quote: Neisser (1967) dubbed the auditory sensory store echoic memory —a term synonymous with auditory sensory memory (ASM).

span.label: short-term store —renamed-across-fields→ working memory
span.note: the quote says the short-term store EVOLVED INTO the working memory construct - a succession over time, not an identity. retyped 2026-08-12 after the same-as transitivity audit. renamed-across-fields is the closest of the eight types but it is wrong in the detail: this is diachronic within one field, not across fields. Cowan2008 in this same corpus spends its length distinguishing the two.
span.quote: Auditory sensory memory is qualitatively different from post-sensory memory processes ( Massaro, 1972 ; Crowder, 1982 ), including Atkinson and Shiffrin’s short-term store, which evolved into the working memory (WM) construct (see, e.g., Logie and Cowan, 2015 ).

span.label: auditory sensory memory —distinct-from→ working memory
span.quote: With brief retention intervals, some memory tasks may be accomplished using ASM—a different construct from WM altogether.

span.label: auditory sensory memory —operationalised-as→ mismatch negativity
span.quote: The widely researched mismatch negativity (MMN) component (see Näätänen, 2000 ) of evoked neural responses to sounds offers a metric of the duration of ASM.

span.label: rehearsal —part-of→ working memory
span.quote: These “working” aspects of WM— active mental manipulation, rehearsal, and reinstatement of information— represent an important functional distinction between WM and ASM.

span.label: two-stimulus comparison tasks —contrasted-with→ serial recall
span.quote: Nonverbal sounds typically are not amenable to recall tasks, because participants would need to respond verbally

span.label: The few-second retention intervals conventionally used in nonverbal auditory two-stimulus comparison tasks are too short to exclude sensory memory, so results credited to working-memory rehearsal may have been driven by the sensory trace instead.
span.quote: Task demands established by methodological decisions about the duration of the retention interval in two-stimulus comparison tasks may have allowed for ASM to affect results that have been attributed to rehearsal in WM.

span.label: Published estimates of the duration of the auditory sensory trace disagree enormously, running from 2 s or less through 3.5 s, 4-5 s, 10 s, 10-15 s, 20 s and 30 s up to possibly 60 s.
span.quote: Though some researchers have estimated it to be 2 s or less ( Crowder, 1976 ; Huron and Parncutt, 1993 ), longer estimates have included 3.5 s ( Mcevoy et al., 1997 ), 4–5 s ( Glucksberg and Cowen, 1970 ), at least several seconds ( Cowan, 1984 ), 10 s ( Sams et al., 1993 ), 10–15 s ( Winkler and Cowan, 2005 ), 20 s ( Watkins and Todres, 1980 ), at least 30 s ( Winkler et al., 2002 ), and possibly up to 60 s ( Engle and Roberts, 1982 ).

span.label: Retention intervals under 5 s fall inside most published estimates of sensory-memory persistence, while intervals of 8-10 s or more begin to exceed most of them.
span.quote: Intervals of less than 5 s are well within the persistence of many estimates of the behavioral life of ASM, whereas intervals of 8–10 s or more begin to exceed the duration of many, but not all, estimates of the duration of ASM.

span.label: No single safe retention interval can be recommended, because the duration of the sensory trace itself differs considerably from person to person.
span.quote: To complicate the matter further, evidence has suggested that the duration of ASM is subject to considerable individual differences (e.g., Kubovy and Howard, 1976 ).

span.label: White noise produced no suffix effect for either digits or tones, so the noise bursts researchers append to to-be-remembered sounds cannot be assumed to erase the sensory trace.
span.quote: Greene and Samuel (1986) showed that white noise did not result in a suffix effect for verbal digits or non-speech tones, which casts doubt on the effectiveness of white noise as a stimulus that overwrites ASM.

span.label: Articulatory suppression impaired memory for nonverbal sounds at a 6 s retention interval in one study but produced essentially no effect in a comparable study using 3 s and 12 s intervals.
span.quote: Using a similar procedure with a retention interval of 6 s, however, Siedenburg and McAdams (2016) reported that articulatory suppression did impair memory performance compared to a control condition.

span.label: Verbal serial recall separates the two stores by serial position - primacy indexes rehearsal in working memory and auditory recency indexes sensory memory - a dissociation that nonverbal comparison tasks cannot deliver.
span.quote: Analysis of memory for each list position permits dissociations of performance driven by WM rehearsal processes (e.g., primacy effects—recall advantages in the early portion of lists due to extended rehearsal time) from performance driven by ASM (e.g., auditory recency—better recall for the last few items with auditory presentation).

span.label: Four incompatible mechanisms are currently proposed for working memory of nonverbal sounds: the verbal phonological loop, a separate music memory loop, attention, and different mechanisms for pitch versus timbre.
span.quote: Researchers have suggested WM for nonverbal sounds is accomplished by: (1) the phonological loop of verbal WM ( Baddeley and Logie, 1992 ); (2) an independent “music memory loop” ( Berz, 1995 ); (3) attention ( Siedenburg and McAdams, 2016 ); and (4) different mechanisms for pitch versus timbre ( Soemer and Saito, 2015 ).

span.label: The comment attributes the field's contradictory results and its proliferation of rival theories to the conflation of sensory memory with working memory.
span.quote: This conflation of different constructs may be one contributor to discrepant research findings and the resulting proliferation of theoretical conjectures regarding mechanisms of working memory for nonverbal sounds.

span.label: Estimates of how long auditory sensory memory lasts range from under 2 seconds to as much as 60 - the field disagrees with itself by a factor of thirty on the number the whole method depends on.
span.quote: Though some researchers have estimated it to be 2 s or less ( Crowder, 1976 ; Huron and Parncutt, 1993 ), longer estimates have included 3.5 s ( Mcevoy et al., 1997 ), 4–5 s ( Glucksberg and Cowen, 1970 ), at least several seconds ( Cowan, 1984 ), 10 s ( Sams et al., 1993 ), 10–15 s ( Winkler and Cowan, 2005 ), 20 s ( Watkins and Todres, 1980 ), at least 30 s ( Winkler et al., 2002 ), and possibly up to 60 s ( Engle and Roberts, 1982 ).

span.label: Neural evidence puts the sensory trace at up to 20 seconds or longer - far beyond the retention intervals in routine use.
span.quote: In a review of MMN studies, Schröger (2007) concluded that ASM may endure up to 20 s or longer.

span.label: Published studies have called retention of a sound 'working memory' after intervals as short as one second.
span.quote: Golubock and Janata (2013) defined retention of a sound for as brief as 1 s following stimulation as a WM task.

span.label: The verbal working-memory literature did separate the two contributions; the nonverbal literature did not.
span.quote: Thus, in the verbal WM literature, the respective contributions of WM rehearsal and ASM have been disentangled in empirical investigations and their accompanying theoretical interpretations (see Jones et al., 2004 , 2006 ).

span.label: echoic memory / auditory sensory memory (ASM)
span.quote: Neisser (1967) dubbed the auditory sensory store echoic memory —a term synonymous with auditory sensory memory (ASM).

span.label: ASM as a passive store holding a "synthesized auditory memory"
span.term: ASM as a passive store holding a "synthesized auditory memory"
span.quote: Thus, ASM is a passive store of just-heard sounds that retains a “synthesized auditory memory” ( Massaro, 1975 )—a set of acoustic features organized in time that can be consulted to complete behavioral tasks, including comparing sounds to one another (e.g., Crowder, 1982 ).

span.label: the four established properties of ASM: modality-specific, high-resolution, limited in duration, attention-independent
span.term: the four established properties of ASM: modality-specific, high-resolution, limited in duration, attention-independent
span.quote: Contemporary research has established that ASM is: (1) auditory modality-specific; (2) high in resolution, which seems to indicate storage of episodic rather than categorical or abstract information; (3) limited in duration; and (4) independent from attentional processes

span.label: working memory (WM)
span.quote: WM receives input from sensory memory about recent perceptual experiences, maintains and manipulates information during in-progress cognitive activities, and interfaces with long-term memory to reinstate information from the latent, permanent corpus of previous experiences.

span.label: two-stimulus comparison task
span.quote: These studies often have used two-stimulus comparison tasks: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded.

span.label: retention interval
span.quote: The duration of the retention interval—the time during which the initial sound must be remembered—typically has been a few seconds.

span.label: auditory suffix effect
span.quote: The auditory version of the suffix effect—whereby memory for the last few items in auditory serial lists is impaired by presentation of a post-list sound—has been taken to reflect interference in ASM

span.label: auditory sensory memory / echoic memory
span.quote: Neisser (1967) dubbed the auditory sensory store echoic memory —a term synonymous with auditory sensory memory (ASM).

span.label: auditory sensory memory, as a passive store
span.term: auditory sensory memory, as a passive store
span.quote: Thus, ASM is a passive store of just-heard sounds that retains a “synthesized auditory memory” ( Massaro, 1975 )

span.label: the working aspects of working memory
span.term: the working aspects of working memory
span.quote: These “working” aspects of WM— active mental manipulation, rehearsal, and reinstatement of information— represent an important functional distinction between WM and ASM.

span.label: the Atkinson and Shiffrin three-store model
span.term: the Atkinson and Shiffrin three-store model
span.quote: Atkinson and Shiffrin’s (1968) influential memory model described a sensory register , a short-term store , and a long-term store .

span.label: 3–5 s — the brief retention interval typically separating the two sounds in these comparison tasks
span.quote: These studies often have used two-stimulus comparison tasks: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded.

span.label: 2 s — the maximum sensory-trace duration originally assumed, which licensed treating any longer interval as sensory-memory-free
span.quote: Researchers initially speculated that the maximum duration of the ASM trace was about 2 s or less (e.g., Neisser, 1967 ; Crowder, 1976 ), which suggested that negligible contributions of ASM to memory performance could be assumed when intervals exceeded 2 s.

span.label: 20 s — the sensory-memory duration a review of mismatch-negativity studies concluded was possible
span.quote: In a review of MMN studies, Schröger (2007) concluded that ASM may endure up to 20 s or longer.

span.label: 5 s — the retention interval used in the seminal tonal-memory studies that set the convention
span.quote: For example, Deutsch’s seminal studies of tonal memory (reviewed in Deutsch, 1975 ) used 5 s retention intervals.

span.label: 1 s — the shortest post-stimulus retention that a recent study still labelled a working-memory task
span.quote: Golubock and Janata (2013) defined retention of a sound for as brief as 1 s following stimulation as a WM task.

span.label: 200 ms — duration of the white-noise burst used as a post-stimulus mask intended to overwrite the sensory trace
span.quote: Soemer and Saito used a 200 ms burst of white noise following their to-be-remembered stimuli.

span.label: 8–10 s — the interval length at which retention begins to exceed most estimates of sensory-memory persistence
span.quote: Intervals of less than 5 s are well within the persistence of many estimates of the behavioral life of ASM, whereas intervals of 8–10 s or more begin to exceed the duration of many, but not all, estimates of the duration of ASM.

span.label: 3–5 s — the conventional retention interval in two-stimulus comparison tasks - the number the critique is about
span.quote: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded

span.label: 2 s to 60 s — the full range of published estimates for the duration of auditory sensory memory
span.quote: Though some researchers have estimated it to be 2 s or less ( Crowder, 1976 ; Huron and Parncutt, 1993 ), longer estimates have included 3.5 s ( Mcevoy et al., 1997 ), 4–5 s ( Glucksberg and Cowen, 1970 ), at least several seconds ( Cowan, 1984 ), 10 s ( Sams et al., 1993 ), 10–15 s ( Winkler and Cowan, 2005 ), 20 s ( Watkins and Todres, 1980 ), at least 30 s ( Winkler et al., 2002 ), and possibly up to 60 s ( Engle and Roberts, 1982 ).

span.label: 20 s or longer — duration of the sensory trace as estimated from mismatch negativity studies
span.quote: In a review of MMN studies, Schröger (2007) concluded that ASM may endure up to 20 s or longer.

span.label: 1 s — the shortest interval a published study has called working memory
span.quote: Golubock and Janata (2013) defined retention of a sound for as brief as 1 s following stimulation as a WM task.

span.label: duration of the retention interval between the two sounds
span.term: duration of the retention interval between the two sounds
span.quote: two sounds separated by a brief retention interval (often 3–5 s) are compared, and a “same” or “different” judgment is recorded

span.label: which memory construct the task performance can be attributed to
span.term: which memory construct the task performance can be attributed to
span.quote: Interpretation of observed memory performance for Retention Interval A is ambiguous—participants’ memory performance could reflect the fidelity of the ASM trace, the fidelity of the representation rehearsed in WM, or some combination of information from both sources.
